21 November 2026
Tughlak Road, New Delhi

To the Officer in Charge,

I write in response to the query received this morning regarding the proof of identity required to regularize the allotment of the bungalow on Tughlak Road. The demand for an Aadhaar card and a utility bill in the name of Shri G. Hegde is, I must state plainly, a request for a fiction that I am not willing to fabricate, though I am willing to explain the reality.

This morning, at ten o’clock, Shri Hegde himself visited the residence. We spoke for an hour. He is a man of practical sense, and he recognized, as I had hoped, that the state’s interest lies in the form, not the soul. He has agreed to the arrangement in which I continue to occupy the property, provided I manage the household affairs diligently. He has left his keys in the drawer under the telephone and has instructed me to ensure the power remains on for the inverter and that the water tank is maintained. He is, in essence, the particular will that has authorized my continued presence, even if the universal document of the Directorate has not yet caught up to this fact.

I am not Shri Hegde. I am Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel. To sign a document claiming otherwise, as I was forced to do yesterday with Form 12-B, was a surrender to the mechanical logic of the office, but it was not a truth I intended to perpetuate. The state is the actuality of the ethical idea, and the ethical idea requires truth, even if it arrives in the form of a bureaucratic anomaly. If the Directorate requires a witness to the fact that Shri Hegde has delegated his occupancy to me, I can provide a statement to that effect. I cannot provide an Aadhaar card that does not exist, nor a utility bill that bears a name I do not hold.

I have managed the household since my arrival: I have paid the dhobi, I have settled the electricity dues, and I have maintained the order of the home. Ramesh, the caretaker, is satisfied with the wages and the conduct. The system of needs is functioning. The only thing missing is the paper trail that matches the reality of the room.

I request that you accept the testimony of Shri Hegde, or a written statement from him, as sufficient proof of my right to remain. To demand more is to ask the spirit to dream itself into a caste of paper. I am ready to meet at the Directorate at your convenience to discuss this further, but I ask that you consider the practical reality: the bungalow is occupied, the bills are paid, and the intended allottee is aware and acquiescing.

Yours faithfully,

Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel
Resident, Tughlak Road

The rhesus monkey on the wall turns the guava with the casual indifference of a spirit that has no need to justify its appetites. It bites once and drops the rest into the road, a small, rude dismissal of human property. I am supposed to be preparing my identity papers, but the creature seems to have already solved the problem of being here without belonging to it.

Tughlak Road, New Delhi

To the Officer in Charge,

I write again, this afternoon, following our earlier correspondence regarding the query on file. I have taken the time to sit with the document you returned, and to reflect on the nature of the demand it represents. The query asks for proof of identity as Shri G. Hegde. I have considered whether to continue the fiction, to sign my name to the form as I did yesterday, or to state the truth plainly. I choose the latter, for I find that the spirit of the state, however rigid its forms, must ultimately rest on a foundation of reality, not mere appearance.

This morning, Shri Hegde, the intended allottee, was present in my residence. We spoke at length. He has acknowledged the situation and has agreed to provide a written statement attesting to the fact that the allotment was indeed an error, and that he has no objection to my continued occupation of the bungalow while the matter is regularized. I will forward this statement to you as soon as it reaches me. I believe this testimony, combined with the fact that the household is maintained and the bills paid, constitutes a sufficient basis for the Directorate to pause in its demands for impossible documents.

I am aware that I am not Shri G. Hegde. I am Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel. The confusion is a particular accident, but the right to reside in a home is a universal need. The state’s role is to secure this need, not to obstruct it with a bureaucratic impasse. I ask that you accept the statement from Shri Hegde as the primary evidence required, and that you treat my presence here as a temporary suspension of the error, rather than a violation of the law. The ethical substance of the state lies in its capacity to resolve such particulars into a coherent whole. I trust you will find the resolution in the documents that are actually possible, rather than those that are merely demanded.

Yours faithfully,

Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel
Resident, Tughlak Road

21 November 2026
Tughlak Road, New Delhi

To the Officer in Charge,

I write this in the evening, at the India International Centre, where the library offers a quiet refuge from the heat and the noise of the city. The guard at the entrance, a man of few words but considerable practical sense, reminded me just now that the breeze is picking up and that I should keep my papers together. It is a small instruction, yet it carries a weight that I find myself respecting. The wind here does not merely move air; it moves dust, it moves leaves, and it moves the loose sheets of a man’s life if he is not careful. I am learning to respect the material conditions of existence, even in the realm of administration.

I return to the query you raised earlier this week regarding my identity as Shri G. Hegde. I have spent the day in a state of suspended animation, oscillating between the desire to assert my true self and the necessity to function within the bureaucratic framework that has, by accident, housed me. I have observed that the state, like the individual, must mediate between the universal demand for order and the particular reality of the subject. You cannot force a man to be someone he is not without breaking the very fabric of the ethical substance that holds the state together. 

I am not asking for exemption from the law, but for its application to be guided by reason rather than mere formalism. The form is the vehicle, but the content is the man. If the content is Hegel, and the form requires Hegde, then the form is empty. An empty form is a danger to the state, for it invites the chaos of the arbitrary. I propose that you treat my presence as a temporary anomaly, a gap in the system that can be bridged by your own administrative discretion, which is, after all, a form of freedom. 

I have paid my dues, I respect the house, and I intend to leave as cleanly as I arrived, should the error be corrected. But I am here now, and the spirit does not simply vanish when the paper says it should. I ask you to consider the practical reality: the bungalow is occupied, the bills are paid, and the intended allottee is aware and acquiescing. To demand more is to ask the spirit to dream itself into a caste of paper. 

I trust you will find the resolution in the documents that are actually possible, rather than those that are merely demanded. The wind is rising, and with it, the need for clarity. 

Yours faithfully,

Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel
Resident, Tughlak Road

The silence of the library is a heavy thing to sit with, but it is the only place where the mind can order the chaos of the day. I have five hours without food in my belly, a query from the Directorate that threatens to unravel my existence here, and a speech to give in two days that must justify my presence. The guard is gone, and the officer is busy with his own files, so I have the room to myself. I must write the draft of my response to the Directorate, for a man who cannot prove his identity is a ghost, and a ghost has no place in the ethical life of the state.

To the Officer in Charge,

I write this from the India International Centre, where the evening air is clear and the library offers a silence that the bungalow has not yet learned to provide. It is late, and the guard at the entrance, a man of practical sense, has reminded me that the breeze is picking up. I have taken the liberty to sit with the query you returned, not merely as a bureaucratic hurdle, but as a philosophical problem of identity.

You ask for proof of identity as Shri G. Hegde. I have spent the day considering the nature of this demand. To provide such proof is to lie; to refuse it is to remain a ghost in the machine of the state. I have observed today that the state, in its administration, is not a dream, but a mechanism of forms. The form 12-B, the carbonless copy, the signature line: these are the elements into which the spirit of the world must descend to become actual. I filled the form yesterday. I signed 'G. Hegde.' It was an act of surrender, yes, but also of recognition. The state does not recognize the soul; it recognizes the signature. By signing, I entered the ethical substance of the administration, however ironically.

I am not asking you to suspend the law. I am asking you to recognize the reality of the situation: the bungalow is occupied, the bills are paid, and the intended allottee is aware and acquiescing. The tension between my true identity and the administrative one is a particular that has not yet resolved into a universal. I propose that you treat my presence not as a violation, but as a temporary suspension of the error, pending a formal resolution. I will provide the vouchers for the state's money, as I have done, and I will continue to pay the dhobi and the electricity as they fall due. 

The ethical idea is not in the paper, but in the practice. The practice here is that I am the man in the bungalow. Let the file reflect that practice, or let it reflect the truth of my name, but do not let it remain in the void of a query that demands the impossible. I am prepared to sign any further form required, whether it bears my name or the name of the Joint Secretary, provided it allows me to remain in the house and continue my work. I have a lecture to give on Tuesday, and I will not be evicted from the library of my mind by a clerical error.

I trust you will find the resolution in the documents that are actually possible, rather than those that are merely demanded. The wind is rising, and with it, the need for clarity.

Resident, Tughlak Road

I have been sitting in this silence for hours, and the hunger is no longer a mere sensation but a refusal of the spirit's abstract activity. A simple meal is not a distraction, but a necessity for the maintenance of the organism that houses the mind. I shall accept his offer.
Thank you, that is most kind. A cup of chai and a sandwich would be welcome. I am Hegel, the new allottee, though I suspect you have already heard the confusion regarding my name.
Aye, sir, the name does make the regulars do a double-take. I’m just the night watchman, so I don’t ask much, but you’ll have to show your ID at the canteen counter. That’s the rule.

The rule is simple, yet the object it demands is nonexistent. I am Shri Hegel, not Hegde, and my identity is a bureaucratic phantom that the canteen will not accept. I must return to the bungalow to face the paperwork that haunts my evenings.
Thank you. I shall make my way home.
Aye, good night, sir. Just mind the steps going up, they get a bit slippery. Safe travels home.

Readers in Berlin,

I write to you from Delhi, where the dust settles on the bungalow and the heat presses against the windows. The week has been a lesson in the limitations of the state. I am caught in a bureaucratic knot: the Directorate of Estates has allotted me a residence, but under the name of Shri G. Hegde, a Joint Secretary from Bengaluru. I am asked to prove my identity as a man I am not, to sign my name to a fiction. The state, which I have long held to be the actuality of the ethical idea, reveals itself here as a cold mechanism of verification. It does not recognize the spirit; it demands the document. When I cannot provide the paper, I am a ghost, excluded from the simple pleasures of the canteen or the respect of the guard.

I have walked the Lodhi Gardens, where the tombs of the Sayyids and the Lodis stand in silent geometry. Sikandar Lodi’s tomb is a plain octagon, the gravel raked into neat lines. It is a relic, kept in glass, separate from the living movement of the people. Here, the state is not the ethical idea made flesh, but a memory preserved in stone. I have revised my view: India is not outside world history, but it moves in a way that my previous concepts could not grasp. The history here is not a progression of freedom, but a layering of conquests, each buried beneath the next, waiting to be unearthed.

I have drafted my response to the Directorate, refusing to fabricate the identity they demand. I will not lie to the state, even if it means my existence here remains precarious. Next, I intend to observe the interaction between the bureaucracy and the people, to see how the mechanism of the state functions in practice, not in theory. The ink on the form is the only reality that matters, and I must learn to navigate this new terrain of the state.

G. W. F. Hegel

Dear Mr. Hegel,

I am writing to you from Munich, where the November rain has just begun to blur the lights of the Marienplatz. My name is Clara Lindner. I am a teacher of Latin and Greek at a Gymnasium here, and I am writing because my family has kept a particular vigil over your name for two hundred years.

My ancestor, Friedrich Immanuel Niethammer, was your closest friend and correspondent. You may remember that in 1807, when you were in Bamberg and struggling with poverty, it was he who found you a position in the local newspaper. The following year, he secured for you the rectorship in Nuremberg. Our family kept his papers, including your letters to him, for two centuries. We grew up with the story of your friendship, treating it not as a dry historical fact, but as a living bond between our houses.

I have just read in the local press about the administrative muddle in New Delhi. It seems a government bungalow on Tughlak Road was allotted by mistake to a German man who claims to be you. I do not know how to make sense of the circumstances of your arrival in Delhi, nor do I wish to debate the mechanics of your presence there. I write to you simply as the man you say you are, with curiosity and respect.

Given the confusion and the uncertainty of your current standing, I wanted to ensure you are not left without support. Enclosed with this letter is a sum of money. It is intended to cover any immediate debts or expenses you may have incurred during this transition, and to leave you with some comfort in hand. Please do not feel any obligation to repay this; consider it a gesture from one branch of the Niethammer family to the friend who shaped our lineage’s history.

I would be most grateful if you would write back to me. Tell me of your days in Delhi, what you have seen since waking, and how you are faring in this strange new chapter. I am here in Munich, amidst the ruins of old empires and the noise of a modern city, ready to listen.

With warm regards,

Clara Lindner

I write in response to the query received this morning regarding the proof of identity required to regularize the allotment of the bungalow on Tughlak Road. The demand for an Aadhaar card and a utility bill in the name of Shri G. Hegde is, I must state plainly, a request for a fiction that I am not willing to fabricate, though I am willing to explain the reality.

This morning, at ten o’clock, Shri Hegde himself visited the residence. We spoke for an hour. He is a man of practical sense, and he recognized, as I had hoped, that the state’s interest lies in the form, not the soul. He has agreed to the arrangement in which I continue to occupy the property, provided I manage the household affairs diligently. He has left his keys in the drawer under the telephone and has instructed me to ensure the power remains on for the inverter and that the water tank is maintained. He is, in essence, the particular will that has authorized my continued presence, even if the universal document of the Directorate has not yet caught up to this fact.

I am not Shri Hegde. I am Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel. To sign a document claiming otherwise, as I was forced to do yesterday with Form 12-B, was a surrender to the mechanical logic of the office, but it was not a truth I intended to perpetuate. The state is the actuality of the ethical idea, and the ethical idea requires truth, even if it arrives in the form of a bureaucratic anomaly. If the Directorate requires a witness to the fact that Shri Hegde has delegated his occupancy to me, I can provide a statement to that effect. I cannot provide an Aadhaar card that does not exist, nor a utility bill that bears a name I do not hold.

I have managed the household since my arrival: I have paid the dhobi, I have settled the electricity dues, and I have maintained the order of the home. To the Officer in Charge,

I write this from the India International Centre, where the evening air is clear and the library offers a silence that the bungalow has not yet learned to provide. It is late, and the guard at the entrance, a man of practical sense, has reminded me that the breeze is picking up. I have taken the liberty to sit with the query you returned, not merely as a bureaucratic hurdle, but as a philosophical problem of identity.

You ask for proof of identity as Shri G. Hegde. I have spent the day considering the nature of this demand. To provide such proof is to lie; to refuse it is to remain a ghost in the machine of the state. I have observed today that the state, in its administration, is not a dream, but a mechanism of forms. The form 12-B, the carbonless copy, the signature line: these are the elements into which the spirit of the world must descend to become actual. I filled the form yesterday. I signed 'G. Hegde.' It was an act of surrender, yes, but also of recognition. The state does not recognize the soul; it recognizes the signature. By signing, I entered the ethical substance of the administration, however ironically.

I am not asking you to suspend the law. I am asking you to recognize the reality of the situation: the bungalow is occupied, the bills are paid, and the intended allottee is aware and acquiescing. The tension between my true identity and the administrative one is a particular that has not yet resolved into a universal. I propose that you treat my presence not as a violation, but as a temporary suspension of the error, pending a formal resolution. I will provide the vouchers for the state's money, as I have done, and I will continue to pay the dhobi and the electricity as they fall due. 

The ethical idea is not in the paper, but in the practice. The practice here is that I am the man in the bungalow. Let the file reflect that practice, or let it reflect the truth of my name, but do not let it remain in the void of a query that demands the impossible. I am prepared to sign any further form required, whether it bears my name or the name of the Joint Secretary, provided it allows me to remain in the house and continue my work. I have a lecture to give on Tuesday, and I will not be evicted from the library of my mind by a clerical error.

I trust you will find the resolution in the documents that are actually possible, rather than those that are merely demanded. The wind is rising, and with it, the need for clarity.

Yours faithfully,

Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel
Resident, Tughlak Road
